questions.stem: A 13-year-old girl returns to clinic 2 weeks after being treated for streptococcal pharyngitis. Her mother reports that the patient's face became puffy 2 days ago and her urine has turned the color of cola. Her blood pressure is 130/90 mm Hg, and she has periorbital and 2+ lower extremity edema. Which clinical syndrome best describes her presentation?
explanations: Incorrect. Nephrotic syndrome features heavy proteinuria and hypoalbuminemia; PIGN seldom reaches the nephrotic range.
Correct. PIGN classically presents as nephritic syndrome with hematuria, hypertension, and edema following an extrarenal infection.
Incorrect. ATN follows ischemic or toxic insults and shows muddy brown casts, not hematuria after a streptococcal infection.
Incorrect. Renal artery stenosis causes hypertension but not hematuria or edema after pharyngitis.
Incorrect. Hepatorenal syndrome occurs in advanced liver disease, not after strep throat.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old boy develops gross hematuria, hypertension, and periorbital edema 2 weeks after a sore throat. Which organism is the most common cause of his condition?
explanations: Incorrect. Staphylococci are an increasingly common cause, especially in adults, but are not the most common overall.
Correct. Group A beta-hemolytic Streptococcus (S. pyogenes) is the most common cause of PIGN, producing poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis.
Incorrect. E. coli is not a typical PIGN trigger.
Incorrect. S. pneumoniae is not the classical cause of PIGN; group A strep is.
Incorrect. Mycoplasma is not a typical cause of PIGN in this brick.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old child with impetigo 4 weeks ago presents with cola-colored urine and edema. According to the brick, what is the typical interval between a streptococcal skin infection and the onset of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
explanations: Incorrect. This interval is too short; PSGN takes weeks to develop.
Incorrect. 1 to 3 weeks is the interval after pharyngitis, not skin infection.
Incorrect. This delay is far too long for PSGN.
Incorrect. PSGN does not typically develop months later.
Correct. PSGN typically appears 3 to 6 weeks after a streptococcal skin infection such as impetigo or cellulitis.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old girl develops nephritic syndrome 2 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. According to the brick, what is the typical interval between strep throat and the onset of poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
explanations: Incorrect. PSGN does not present at the time of acute pharyngitis.
Incorrect. This interval is too short.
Correct. After streptococcal pharyngitis, PSGN typically appears 1 to 3 weeks later.
Incorrect. 3 to 6 weeks is the interval seen after a strep skin infection.
Incorrect. This delay is far too long.

questions.stem: An 8-year-old boy with PIGN has biopsy findings of granular IgG and C3 deposits along the glomerular basement membrane. Which immune mechanism best explains the glomerular injury?
explanations: Incorrect. Type I (IgE-mediated) reactions cause allergy and anaphylaxis, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Type II involves antibodies against fixed cell-surface antigens, not deposited immune complexes.
Correct. PIGN is a type III hypersensitivity reaction in which circulating immune complexes deposit in the glomerulus and activate complement.
Incorrect. Type IV is delayed T-cell mediated injury, not the mechanism in PIGN.
Incorrect. The kidney itself is not infected; injury is immune-mediated, not from direct bacterial invasion.

questions.stem: A 12-year-old with PIGN has serum complement studies sent. Which pattern is most characteristic?
explanations: Correct. PIGN activates the alternative complement pathway, producing low C3 in roughly 90% of cases while C4 is typically normal.
Incorrect. Low C4 with normal C3 suggests classical pathway activation, as in hereditary angioedema.
Incorrect. Low C3 and C4 together suggest classical pathway activation (e.g., lupus nephritis).
Incorrect. C3 is not elevated in PIGN.
Incorrect. Complement is consumed in PIGN, so C3 is typically low.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old has hypocomplementemia after a streptococcal infection. Why is C3 low in PIGN, while C4 is low in hereditary angioedema?
choices: PIGN consumes membrane attack complex only
explanations: Incorrect. The brick attributes PIGN complement consumption to the alternative pathway, not the lectin pathway.
Correct. PIGN immune complexes activate the alternative pathway, bypassing classical components C2 and C4 and selectively consuming C3.
Incorrect. The classical pathway is activated in HAE (loss of C1-INH), explaining its low C4.
Incorrect. Membrane attack complex consumption alone does not explain isolated low C3.
Incorrect. HAE does involve C3, but its hallmark is low C4 from classical pathway overactivation.

questions.stem: A renal biopsy from a child with PIGN is examined under light microscopy. Which finding is most characteristic?
explanations: Incorrect. Sclerosis is a feature of FSGS or chronic injury, not acute PIGN.
Incorrect. Kimmelstiel-Wilson nodules are pathognomonic for diabetic nephropathy.
Incorrect. Diffuse GBM thickening is characteristic of membranous nephropathy.
Incorrect. Split (tram-track) basement membranes are seen in membranoproliferative GN and Alport syndrome.
Correct. PIGN shows enlarged, hypercellular glomeruli with proliferation of endothelial and mesangial cells plus an influx of neutrophils and monocytes.

questions.stem: Immunofluorescence on a renal biopsy from a patient with PIGN reveals a granular pattern of IgG and C3 along the GBM and mesangium. What is this appearance commonly called?
explanations: Incorrect. Tram-track describes split basement membranes in membranoproliferative GN.
Incorrect. A linear pattern is characteristic of anti-GBM disease, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Spike-and-dome is the EM pattern of membranous nephropathy.
Correct. The granular IgG and C3 deposits in PIGN produce a 'starry sky' immunofluorescence appearance.
Incorrect. Wire-loop lesions are seen in lupus nephritis.

questions.stem: Electron microscopy from a child with PIGN shows scattered dome-shaped electron-dense deposits. Where along the glomerular basement membrane are these deposits located?
explanations: Incorrect. Subendothelial deposits are typical of lupus nephritis and MPGN, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Intramembranous deposits are seen in dense deposit disease.
Correct. PIGN shows characteristic subepithelial 'humps' on the urinary side of the GBM, away from the capillary lumen.
Incorrect. Mesangial deposits occur but the classic 'humps' are subepithelial.
Incorrect. Deposits are along the GBM, not within podocyte foot processes.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with cola-colored urine, periorbital edema, and recent strep throat has urinalysis sent. Which finding most strongly supports a glomerular source of bleeding?
explanations: Incorrect. WBC casts indicate interstitial nephritis or pyelonephritis.
Incorrect. Hyaline casts are nonspecific and seen in normal or volume-depleted patients.
Incorrect. Calcium oxalate crystals point to nephrolithiasis or ethylene glycol toxicity.
Incorrect. Bacteria and nitrites suggest urinary tract infection, not glomerular disease.
Correct. Dysmorphic RBCs and RBC casts indicate glomerular bleeding and are classic for PIGN.

questions.stem: A 14-year-old presents with cola-colored urine and edema 3 weeks after a sore throat. No throat culture was performed at the time. Which serologic test best supports a recent streptococcal infection?
explanations: Incorrect. ANA screens for systemic lupus, not streptococcal infection.
Correct. Antistreptolysin O titer (and the Streptozyme panel) detect antibodies against streptococcal antigens and confirm recent streptococcal infection.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM antibody is the marker for Goodpasture disease.
Incorrect. ANCA is associated with pauci-immune vasculitides like GPA and MPA.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA is specific for systemic lupus erythematosus.

questions.stem: An 11-year-old presents with hematuria and edema 4 weeks after streptococcal pharyngitis. Why are throat and blood cultures rarely useful for diagnosing poststreptococcal glomerulonephritis?
choices: Strep is too fastidious to culture
The infection has resolved by then
explanations: Incorrect. Group A strep is readily cultured when present.
Incorrect. Cost is not the brick's reason for the limited utility of cultures.
Incorrect. Strep is extracellular and easily cultured during active infection.
Correct. The skin or throat infection occurred 1 to 6 weeks earlier and has typically resolved by the time PSGN is diagnosed, so cultures rarely yield the organism.
Incorrect. While true that the kidney itself is not infected, the brick attributes culture's poor yield to timing of the resolved infection.

questions.stem: A 65-year-old hospitalized man with MRSA endocarditis develops hematuria, hypertension, and a rising creatinine within days of admission. Which form of postinfectious glomerulonephritis is most likely?
explanations: Incorrect. PSGN follows strep infection by weeks, not days, and is more common in children.
Correct. Staphylococcus-associated GN occurs within days of infection in adults with serious infections such as endocarditis, cellulitis, osteomyelitis, or pneumonia.
Incorrect. IgA nephropathy classically presents with synpharyngitic hematuria within days of an upper respiratory infection but is not associated with staph infections.
Incorrect. Anti-GBM disease shows linear IgG deposition and pulmonary-renal syndrome, not staph-related nephritis.
Incorrect. Membranous nephropathy is a nephrotic, not nephritic, disorder.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old man with Staphylococcus-associated glomerulonephritis is being managed in the hospital. According to the brick, what is the most important component of his treatment?
explanations: Incorrect. Plasmapheresis is used for anti-GBM disease, not staph-associated PIGN.
Incorrect. The brick does not recommend steroids as primary therapy for staph-associated PIGN.
Correct. Adults with staph-associated PIGN require prompt antibiotic treatment of the underlying infection to prevent prolonged renal complications.
Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is reserved for severe ANCA vasculitis or lupus, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Biopsy is rarely needed; treatment of the underlying infection should not be delayed for biopsy.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old child with PIGN has mild hypertension and 2+ lower extremity edema. According to the brick, what is the mainstay of management?
explanations: Correct. Treatment of PIGN in children is primarily supportive, since the natural course is short and most resolve within 1 to 2 weeks.
Incorrect. Steroids are not standard for PIGN.
Incorrect. Cyclophosphamide is not used for routine PIGN.
Incorrect. Dialysis is reserved for the rare severe cases with renal failure.
Incorrect. Transplantation is not part of acute PIGN management.

questions.stem: A 10-year-old with PIGN develops worsening lower extremity edema and shortness of breath from volume overload. Which medication is most appropriate for fluid removal?
explanations: Incorrect. Thiazides are weaker diuretics and not the brick's recommended choice for PIGN volume overload.
Incorrect. Spironolactone is potassium-sparing but a weak diuretic for acute volume removal.
Correct. The brick recommends loop diuretics such as furosemide for fluid removal in PIGN.
Incorrect. Mannitol is an osmotic diuretic used for cerebral edema, not PIGN volume overload.
Incorrect. Acetazolamide is a weak diuretic used for altitude sickness or metabolic alkalosis.

questions.stem: An adult with confirmed Staphylococcus-associated glomerulonephritis needs antibiotic therapy. According to the brick, which agent is typically used because of its gram-positive coverage?
explanations: Correct. The brick states that penicillin V is typically used because it provides good gram-positive coverage against the most common bacterial organisms.
Incorrect. Fluoroquinolones primarily cover gram-negative organisms.
Incorrect. Metronidazole covers anaerobes and protozoa, not staph.
Incorrect. While TMP-SMX has some staph activity, the brick names penicillin V.
Incorrect. Acyclovir is an antiviral, not relevant for bacterial PIGN.

questions.stem: A 9-year-old with PSGN is hospitalized. The mother asks how long symptoms will last. According to the brick, when do symptoms typically resolve in children?
explanations: Incorrect. Symptoms do not resolve that quickly.
Incorrect. Resolution typically takes longer than a few days.
Correct. For most children with PIGN, symptoms resolve within 1 to 2 weeks of presentation.
Incorrect. In adults, hematuria can persist 3 to 6 months, but children usually recover much sooner.
Incorrect. Years-long resolution is not typical.

questions.stem: A pediatrician is counseling parents about the prognosis of their 8-year-old daughter's PSGN. According to the brick, what percentage of children with PIGN progress to renal failure?
explanations: Correct. Only about 1% of children with PIGN progress to renal failure; most recover fully.
Incorrect. The brick cites a much lower rate of renal failure in children.
Incorrect. 17% is the rate of progression to ESRD in adults with staph-associated PIGN.
Incorrect. 25% is the rate of persistently decreased GFR in adults with staph-associated PIGN.
Incorrect. PIGN does not lead to renal failure in half of pediatric cases.

questions.stem: A 68-year-old man with Staphylococcus-associated glomerulonephritis is counseled about prognosis. According to the brick, approximately what percentage of adults with staph-associated PIGN progress to end-stage renal disease requiring dialysis or transplantation?
explanations: Incorrect. 1% is the pediatric PIGN rate of renal failure.
Incorrect. The brick cites a higher rate for adult staph-associated disease.
Correct. Adults with staph-associated PIGN have approximately a 17% chance of progressing to ESRD requiring dialysis or transplantation.
Incorrect. The brick does not cite 50% progression to ESRD.
Incorrect. The brick does not cite 75% progression to ESRD.

questions.stem: A 60-year-old man recovers from Staphylococcus-associated glomerulonephritis but follow-up labs continue to show reduced kidney function. Approximately what fraction of adults with staph-associated PIGN have persistently decreased GFR?
explanations: Incorrect. 1% applies to pediatric progression to renal failure.
Incorrect. The brick cites a higher rate.
Incorrect. Most adults do not have such severe persistent disease.
Incorrect. The brick does not cite 50%.
Correct. About 25% of adults with staph-associated PIGN have persistently decreased GFR.

questions.stem: A 50-year-old woman with PIGN is told her hematuria may persist longer than her other symptoms. In adults, how long can hematuria persist after PIGN?
explanations: Incorrect. Hematuria persists longer than hours in adults.
Incorrect. Hematuria persists longer than days in adults.
Incorrect. 1 to 2 weeks is the resolution interval for symptoms overall, particularly in children.
Correct. In adults, the hematuria of PIGN can persist for 3 to 6 months or, less commonly, for years.
Incorrect. While years is possible, the typical persistence cited in the brick is 3 to 6 months.

questions.stem: A 35-year-old woman with PIGN does not improve after 2 weeks and shows declining GFR. According to the brick, what is the appropriate next step?
explanations: Incorrect. Repeat antibiotics will not address persistent disease, especially in non-staph cases.
Correct. If the disease does not reverse in a week or two or is severe (e.g., declining GFR), a renal biopsy is performed to ensure another glomerular disease has not been missed.
Incorrect. Plasmapheresis is used for anti-GBM and severe ANCA vasculitis, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Steroids are not the brick's recommended next step.
Incorrect. Transplantation is not appropriate for acute PIGN.

questions.stem: A 7-year-old boy presents with hematuria, edema, and hypertension 2 weeks after strep throat. Which combination of findings best supports the diagnosis of PIGN?
choices: Low C3, normal C4, RBC casts
Linear IgG on biopsy, low C3
Anti-dsDNA positive, low C3 and C4
explanations: Correct. The classic PIGN combination is low C3 with normal C4 (alternative pathway activation) plus urinalysis showing RBCs and RBC casts.
Incorrect. Eosinophiluria suggests acute interstitial nephritis, not PIGN.
Incorrect. Linear IgG deposition is the hallmark of anti-GBM disease; PIGN shows granular IgG.
Incorrect. Anti-dsDNA with low C3 and C4 indicates lupus nephritis.
Incorrect. ANCA positivity points to pauci-immune vasculitis (e.g., GPA), not PIGN.
